name: onesie-setup
description: Use when onesie is not on PATH, when no API key resolves, when the session start hook reports either, or when the user asks how to install or set up onesie. Walks the user through installing it, choosing a provider and storing a key, without the key ever entering the conversation.
compatibility: Needs a shell. Installing onesie needs Homebrew, curl or a Go toolchain.

rules.short: Never ask for the key in chat. The user stores it with onesie profile create, outside the conversation.
rules.why: Anything typed into the conversation is sent to the model and kept in the transcript. `onesie profile create NAME --provider PROVIDER` reads the key from a hidden prompt in a real terminal, or from stdin otherwise, and never prints it. So ask the user to run it in their own terminal, or to pipe the key from a password manager, as in `pass show typesafe | head -n 1 | onesie profile create work --provider typesafe`. `pass show` and its siblings print metadata after the secret, and `profile create` refuses stdin that holds more than one non blank line, so keep the `head -n 1`. A command that reads from a password manager is safe to run for them, since only stderr lines naming the keychain item or the file come back.

rules.short: Ask which account the user has, TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Berget, Levanto or Cloudflare, before storing a key.
rules.why: A profile names its provider, so `onesie profile create work --provider openrouter` makes an OpenRouter profile. The first profile becomes the default, and a run with no `--profile` uses the default. To switch to another profile, run `onesie profile use NAME`. Do not export `ONESIE_PROVIDER` for a stored key, since `--provider` and `ONESIE_PROVIDER` run without a profile and read only the provider's key variable. For cloudflare, pass the account too, as in `onesie profile create cf --provider cloudflare --account-id ACCOUNT_ID`. `--model` stores the model a run uses when it names none.

rules.short: End the setup with onesie profile test, not profile show.
rules.why: `profile show` only reports what a run would use and where its key lives, and never reads the keychain. `profile test` reads the key and sends it to the provider's model listing, which costs no tokens, then prints `profile:`, `provider:`, `key:` and `models:` with a count. On berget it also asks one tiny question with the profile's model, which spends a few tokens. It exits 2 when no key resolves, 3 when the provider refuses the key or the keychain cannot give it up, and 4 or 5 when the provider cannot be reached. Only a clean `profile test` means the next real command will work.
